Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green) and every gift (red). There is no Aldughaither chapter for brain tumours. The old exam bank filed under "Localization of lesions within the CNS" is mostly spinal (older curriculum) — those questions are at the end, in red. Brain-localization questions were filed under Management of intracranial tumours; they are shown here too (chips marked mx).

Why localization matters

  • The clinical exam is a localizing tool: a tumour's signs and symptoms mirror the function of the brain tissue it disturbs.
  • History + examination generate an anatomical hypothesis before any scan is obtained. That hypothesis focuses imaging review and helps explain findings that don't fit — e.g. a "false localizing" sixth-nerve palsy from raised ICP.
  • Localization also anticipates the functional risk of surgery in that region.
  • The signs a tumour produces depend on WHERE it is, HOW FAST it grows, and its effect on surrounding tissue.
  • Why the clinical hypothesis matters: (1) it directs imaging — guides how the CT/MRI is read; (2) it tests the fit — do the imaging findings actually explain the deficits?; (3) it plans surgery, especially near eloquent cortex.
  • Always consider: side (right vs left; dominant vs non-dominant) · cortex vs white matter (different functions and pathology, e.g. MS = mainly white matter) · eloquent vs silent cortex.
True localizing signFalse localizing sign
Deficit caused directly by dysfunction of the involved anatomical regionDeficit caused by a distant effect (raised ICP / hydrocephalus) — does not point to the tumour site
e.g. contralateral weakness from a precentral lesionCN VI palsy — this nerve is especially vulnerable to pressure/stretch (long intracranial course)

Cerebral lobes & key regions at a glance

RegionFunction
FrontalVoluntary movement, expressive language, executive function & personality
ParietalSomatosensation, spatial awareness, praxis, calculation & language integration
TemporalReceptive language, memory (hippocampus), auditory processing
OccipitalPrimary visual processing
CerebellumCoordination, balance, motor timing
Sellar / pituitaryEndocrine axis, optic chiasm relations

Principles of functional localization

  • Eloquent vs non-eloquent cortex: eloquent areas (motor strip, language, primary visual/sensory cortex) produce deficits when damaged; "silent" areas (e.g. right frontal/temporal pole) may grow large before symptoms appear.
  • Hemispheric dominance: language localizes to the dominant hemisphere (left in ~95% of right-handers) — explains why left temporal/frontal lesions cause aphasia and right-sided ones cause neglect.
  • Language is left-dominant in most people, including > 70% of left-handers; a minority are right or bilateral.
  • Cortex vs white-matter tracts: a lesion can disconnect distant regions by interrupting a tract (e.g. optic radiations, arcuate fasciculus) without directly involving the cortex it affects.
  • Homuncular organization: the motor and sensory strips are somatotopically mapped — a focal deficit (e.g. face–arm predominant) points to a specific point along the strip.
  • Somatotopy: leg/foot most MEDIAL · trunk intermediate · face/tongue most LATERAL.
  • Functional shortcuts: frontal = motor (plus behaviour, executive function, dominant-side speech production) · parietal = somatosensory + spatial · temporal = emotion + memory (plus language comprehension, hearing) · occipital = vision · language network = dominant frontal + temporal/parietal regions.

How a tumour produces symptoms

  • Mass effect & oedema: direct compression and surrounding vasogenic oedema distort adjacent, otherwise normal, brain.
  • Infiltration / destruction: diffusely growing tumours (e.g. glioma) replace and destroy functioning tissue directly.
  • Cortical irritation: abnormal electrical discharge from the tumour margin presents as focal or secondarily generalized seizures.
  • CSF pathway obstruction: tumours near the ventricles/aqueduct/fourth ventricle cause obstructive hydrocephalus → raised ICP.
MechanismWhat happensClinical / surgical meaning
Mass effectCompresses or displaces normal tissue rather than destroying it; white-matter tracts remain intactDeficits may recover after decompression/removal (e.g. extra-axial dominant frontal tumour compressing language cortex → aphasia)
Infiltration & destructionMalignant cells invade cortex and white matter (glioma)Cannot be cleanly separated from functional tissue → resection harder, may destroy tracts
Cortical irritationIrritation of the cortex (not white matter alone)Cortical tumours commonly present with seizures; semiology localizes
Obstruction3rd-ventricle lesion, ventricular compression, mass near the 4th ventricleHydrocephalus → raised ICP; a large "quiet" tumour may present only with headache + vomiting
  • Presentation depends on tumour location · growth rate · degree of compression/infiltration · effect on surrounding tissue and CSF pathways.

Raised intracranial pressure

The Monro–Kellie doctrine

  • The skull is a fixed-volume box. Brain + blood + CSF must sum to a constant — growth of a tumour (or its oedema) must be compensated, or pressure rises.
ComponentShareBehaviour
Brain tissue~80%Displaced by mass effect; compresses last and abruptly once other buffers are exhausted
Blood~10%CSF and venous blood are displaced first — the earliest compensatory buffer
CSF~10%Absorption increases and volume shifts into the spinal thecal sac
  • An increase in one component without adequate compensation → raised ICP → deterioration/herniation. Infants differ: the skull is not yet completely rigid.
  • Tumour patient collapses with high ICP — the pressure–volume relationship → keyed "the curve shifts to the right" (he is on the steep, decompensated part where a small extra volume causes a big rise in pressure). mx 438

Clinical features to recognize

  • Headache — worse in the morning, with coughing/straining (Valsalva), or when lying flat.
  • Vomiting — often without preceding nausea, may be projectile.
  • Papilloedema — blurred disc margins on fundoscopy — always examine the fundus.
  • Sixth (abducens) nerve palsy — a "false localizing sign": the long intracranial course makes CN VI vulnerable to pressure, independent of tumour site.
  • Cushing triad — hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration — a late, pre-terminal sign of impending herniation.
  • Declining consciousness — from drowsiness to coma as compensation fails — a neurosurgical emergency.
  • Cushing's triad = high systolic BP (wide pulse pressure), low HR, low/irregular RR. mx 432
  • Early-morning headache of raised ICP → increased systemic PCO₂ (hypoventilation during sleep → cerebral vasodilatation). mx 434 ×2
  • Other manifestations of an intracranial tumour: motor weakness, hyperreflexia, aphasia, personality/behavioural change, numbness, headache, vomiting, seizures, blurred vision, cognitive decline/dementia, reduced consciousness.
  • Acute deterioration = neurosurgical emergency: large haemorrhage or severe raised ICP → sudden drowsiness → ABC → urgent CT. Any new seizure or focal deficit with suspected intracranial pathology → brain imaging is required.

Seizure semiology can suggest location

  • A new-onset focal seizure in an adult should always raise suspicion for a structural lesion.
  • Focal seizures may remain focal (retained or altered awareness) or secondarily generalize.
  • The seizure semiology — what the patient/witness describes — often points directly to the lobe of origin.
LobeSeizure semiology (slides)Doctor's clue
FrontalMotor jerking, head/eye version, brief with rapid recovery, prominent nocturnal clustersPrimarily motor; brief, rapid, often at night
TemporalAura (déjà vu, epigastric rising, fear, olfactory/gustatory), oral automatisms, behavioural arrestHighly epileptogenic lobe; strange/emotional experiences, abdominal sensation
ParietalContralateral sensory disturbance, tingling or distorted body perceptionLimb feels swollen or twisted; no jerking needed
OccipitalElementary visual hallucinations (flashing lights, colours), forced eye deviationVisual symptoms only (objects/animals not really there)
  • A focal seizure may remain focal, occur with intact awareness, or progress to secondary generalization (e.g. mouth twitching or one-arm twitching). History is critical.

Regional localization

Frontal lobe

  • Anatomy & function: precentral gyrus = primary motor cortex (somatotopic homunculus) · Broca's area (dominant, posterior inferior frontal gyrus) → speech production · prefrontal cortex → executive function, judgement, personality, social behaviour · frontal eye fields → conjugate gaze · orbitofrontal region lies against the olfactory tract.
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Contralateral hemiparesis, often face/arm predominant.
    • Personality and behavioural change — disinhibition, apathy, poor judgement (may mimic psychiatric illness).
    • Expressive (Broca's) aphasia if the dominant hemisphere is involved.
    • Gait apraxia and urinary incontinence with bifrontal/medial lesions.
    • Anosmia with orbitofrontal masses (e.g. olfactory groove meningioma).
    • Contralateral gaze deviation from frontal eye field involvement.
Personality change is easy to misattribute to mood or psychiatric disorder — always consider a frontal mass.
  • Broca area = dominant F3 (inferior frontal gyrus: pars opercularis + pars triangularis; the third division is pars orbitalis). Surgical injury → major language deficit. Supplementary motor area (superior/medial frontal) → motor-association deficit.
  • Bifrontal clue: gait apraxia + urinary incontinence. New psychiatric or personality symptoms can be caused by a frontal tumour — consider an organic cause before labelling them purely psychiatric.
  • Seizure + enhancing lesion of the left inferior frontal lobe → difficulty in expression (Broca / expressive aphasia). mx 437
  • 60-year-old, progressive left-sided weakness (arm > leg) over 3 months + left UMN facial palsy, normal speech → right frontal glioblastoma (progressive = tumour; sudden = stroke). mx 434 ×2
  • Intra-axial heterogeneous enhancing lesion in the right premotor gyrus → high-grade primary brain tumour. mx 437 ×2

Parietal lobe

  • Anatomy & function: postcentral gyrus = primary somatosensory cortex · dominant (usually left) — language integration, calculation, praxis · non-dominant (usually right) — spatial awareness & attention · optic radiation fibres loop through the parietal lobe (superior fibres).
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Contralateral cortical sensory loss — impaired two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, stereognosis.
    • Dominant: Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left–right confusion); ideomotor apraxia; alexia.
    • Non-dominant: hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, constructional apraxia.
    • Inferior contralateral homonymous quadrantanopia (superior optic radiation).
  • Cortical sensory loss: the patient may feel a basic stimulus but cannot interpret it. Gerstmann syndrome is marked MCQ in the doctor's notes; the parietal quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor") is marked EXAM.
  • Non-dominant parietal: normal motor power, yet cannot navigate or interact with the contralateral side of space (spatial disorientation, agnosia, constructional apraxia).

Temporal lobe

  • Anatomy & function: Wernicke's area (dominant, posterior superior temporal gyrus) → language comprehension · hippocampus & mesial structures → memory consolidation · primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) · Meyer's loop — inferior optic radiation fibres sweep through the temporal lobe.
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Receptive aphasia (fluent but nonsensical/paraphasic speech) if dominant hemisphere.
    • Short-term memory impairment with mesial temporal involvement.
    • Complex partial (focal impaired-awareness) seizures with auras — déjà vu, epigastric rising sensation, olfactory/gustatory hallucinations, automatisms.
    • Superior contralateral homonymous quadrantanopia — classic "pie in the sky" (Meyer's loop).
    • Contralateral facial/visual recognition difficulty with select lesions.
  • Hippocampal memory: dominant (left) = verbal; right = non-verbal. The arcuate fasciculus is the white-matter link between Broca and Wernicke.
Broca (expressive)Wernicke (receptive)
LocationDominant inferior frontal gyrus (F3)Dominant temporal lobe
SpeechProduction impaired (non-fluent)Fluent but meaningless / inappropriate
ComprehensionRelatively preservedImpaired; answers fluently with unrelated content

Occipital lobe

  • Anatomy & function: primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus · macular (central) vision has bilateral cortical representation at the occipital pole · association visual cortex → higher-order visual processing.
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, classically with macular sparing (dual blood supply/bilateral pole representation).
    • Elementary visual hallucinations — unformed flashes, shapes, colours (vs the complex hallucinations of temporal lesions).
    • Anton syndrome (cortical blindness with denial/confabulation) if bilateral occipital involvement.
    • Usually preserved motor, sensory and language function — a relatively "silent" region outside vision.
  • Anton syndrome: occipital cortical damage (tumour, trauma, infiltration…) → cortical blindness; the patient cannot see but confabulates and behaves as if vision were intact.

Cerebellum & posterior fossa

  • Anatomy & function: cerebellar hemispheres → coordination of ipsilateral limb movement · vermis (midline) → truncal/axial coordination and gait · the fourth ventricle lies just anterior — small masses here obstruct CSF flow early · brainstem and lower cranial nerves are close neighbours.
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysmetria (past-pointing), intention tremor — hemispheric lesions.
    • Truncal/gait ataxia, wide-based gait — vermian lesions (common in children, e.g. medulloblastoma).
    • Nystagmus, dysarthria (scanning speech), hypotonia.
    • Early obstructive hydrocephalus → raised ICP presents sooner than in supratentorial tumours.
    • Cranial nerve palsies (V–VIII) or long-tract signs if the brainstem is compressed.
Posterior fossa masses cause raised ICP disproportionately early because of proximity to the fourth ventricle.
  • The posterior fossa is a tight compartment with little room to expand. Vermis lesion → cannot sit unsupported or stand (truncal ataxia). Findings to know for the exam: truncal/limb ataxia, wide-based gait, dysmetria, nystagmus, scanning dysarthria, early obstructive hydrocephalus. These tumours are particularly seen in children.
  • 10-year-old girl, headache + unstable gait, past-pointing and pendular reflexes → medulloblastoma of the cerebellum. mx 432 ×5
  • 6-year-old, headache, vomiting, frequent falls, midline posterior fossa tumour → differential medulloblastoma, ependymoma, (pilocytic) astrocytoma. mx 439

Sellar & parasellar region

  • Anatomy & function: the pituitary sits in the sella turcica, capped by the optic chiasm · the cavernous sinuses flank the sella — contain CN III, IV, VI and V1/V2 · anterior pituitary secretes ACTH, TSH, GH, LH/FSH, prolactin · posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin.
  • Tumour presentation:
    • Bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression (classic sellar visual-field defect).
    • Endocrine dysfunction — hypopituitarism (fatigue, hypogonadism) or hormone excess (e.g. prolactinoma → amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea; acromegaly; Cushing disease).
    • Headache from dural stretch, independent of a discrete raised-ICP mechanism.
    • Cavernous sinus extension → ophthalmoplegia (CN III/IV/VI) and facial numbness (V1/V2).
    • Pituitary apoplexy: sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia — a neurosurgical emergency.
  • The cavernous sinus also contains the internal carotid artery. Prolactinoma: female → menstrual irregularity (amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea); male → impotence + reduced libido.
  • Pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm (visual loss + disturbed menses) → bitemporal hemianopia. mx 437 ×6
  • Headache, visual changes and bilateral milky nipple discharge → serum TSH and prolactin. mx 441

Localization at a glance

RegionMotor / sensoryCognitive / behaviouralVisual fieldOther clues
FrontalContralateral weaknessPersonality change, expressive aphasia (dom.)Gaze deviationIncontinence, anosmia
ParietalCortical sensory lossGerstmann (dom.), neglect (non-dom.)Inferior quadrantanopiaApraxia, alexia
Temporal—Receptive aphasia (dom.), memory lossSuperior quadrantanopiaComplex partial seizures, auras
Occipital—Usually preservedHomonymous hemianopia (macular sparing)Elementary hallucinations
CerebellumAtaxia, dysmetriaUsually preserved—Early hydrocephalus, nystagmus
Sellar—Endocrine dysfunctionBitemporal hemianopiaCN III/IV/VI palsy if cavernous sinus

Imaging

The role of CT

  • Fast, widely available, and excellent for bone and acute haemorrhage — the first-line study in the emergency setting.
When it is used firstWhat it shows wellLimitations
Acute presentation — new focal deficit, seizure, depressed consciousnessAcute haemorrhage, calcification, bone erosion/hyperostosisLower soft-tissue contrast than MRI
Suspected raised ICP or herniation before further work-upHydrocephalus and midline shiftPosterior fossa/brainstem obscured by beam-hardening artefact
Trauma, or when MRI is unavailable/contraindicatedGross mass effect and oedema (with contrast for enhancement)Ionizing radiation, iodinated contrast risk (renal function, allergy)
  • Brain tumour suspected — the study to perform primarily → CT scan. mx 429 ×3

The role of MRI

  • Superior soft-tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging make MRI the definitive study for characterizing and surgically planning around a tumour.
SequenceWhat it tells you
T1 ± gadoliniumAnatomy; enhancement pattern suggests blood–brain-barrier breakdown / tumour grade
T2 / FLAIROedema, infiltration, non-enhancing tumour extent (FLAIR suppresses CSF signal)
DWI / ADCRestricted diffusion — helps distinguish abscess, lymphoma, or highly cellular tumour
GRE / SWIBlood products and calcification (susceptibility artefact)
Advanced: perfusion, spectroscopy, fMRI, tractographyGrading, metabolic profile, and pre-surgical mapping of eloquent cortex/white-matter tracts
  • MRI is contraindicated in some patients (e.g. pacemaker) and less suited to rapid emergency triage.

CT or MRI — choosing the first study

Choose CT when…Choose MRI when…
Acute deterioration or suspected herniationDefinitive characterization of a known/suspected tumour
Trauma work-upPre-operative surgical planning
Rapid triage in the emergency departmentAssessing posterior fossa or brainstem lesions
MRI is contraindicated (e.g. certain implants) or unavailableFollowing tumour response over time (e.g. at 3 months)
Assessing bone involvement / calcificationFunctional mapping near eloquent cortex
  • Clinical localization comes first; imaging then confirms. Do not assign detailed function from the CT appearance alone — always correlate with the clinical findings.
  • High-yield emergency scenario (OSCE/MCQ): previously healthy 25-year-old, severe headache + nausea/vomiting → 2 hours later acute drop in consciousness → ABC → urgent CT → MRI for definitive localization. A patient with chronic headache/migraine who develops a new deterioration or change in pattern needs reassessment for secondary intracranial pathology.
  • Treated lung SCC, now headache, vomiting and left upper-limb weakness → MRI brain showing a right frontal lesion (metastasis; the lesion is contralateral to the weakness). mx 439 ×2

Key takeaways

  • Presentation reflects function: mass effect, infiltration, irritation, or CSF obstruction.
  • Raised ICP has a recognizable syndrome — headache, vomiting, papilloedema, and (late) Cushing triad.
  • Each lobe has a signature deficit pattern — use the exam to build an anatomical hypothesis.
  • CT triages acutely; MRI defines and plans around the lesion.
  • Always correlate the clinical localization with imaging before finalizing a surgical plan.

Cases

Case 1 — frontal lobe mass

  • History: progressive personality change and one witnessed focal motor seizure. MRI obtained for work-up.
  • Examination: mild disinhibition and flattened affect · subtle contralateral pronator drift · non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension (dominant hemisphere) · no visual-field deficit.
Personality change + focal seizure + an enhancing frontal mass → frontal lobe.

Case 2 — posterior fossa mass

  • History: a child with several weeks of early-morning headache and vomiting, and a new unsteady, wide-based gait.
  • Examination: papilloedema · truncal ataxia — unable to tandem walk · dysmetria on finger-to-nose · no focal limb weakness; cranial nerves intact.

A posterior fossa mass effacing the fourth ventricle (left), with resulting dilatation of the lateral ventricles — obstructive hydrocephalus (right)

Truncal ataxia + early raised ICP in a child → classic for a posterior fossa tumour causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

Additional imaging examples

Doctor's clinical localization examples

CaseKey featuresLocalization / action
Bifrontal tumourProgressive memory/executive decline, falling work performance, difficulty writing/organizing, disinhibition, urinary incontinenceBifrontal involvement — not an isolated psychiatric disorder
Paediatric tumour with hydrocephalus (13 y)Headache, worsening school performance, severe oedema, ventricular obstruction, gait so impaired the child needs parental helpTumour resection + EVD for CSF diversion (gait + early hydrocephalus in a child → posterior fossa)
Tumour haemorrhageTumour bleeds acutely → rapid neurological deteriorationA planned elective/awake procedure can become an emergency operation
Right parietal tumour (65 y)Difficulty walking without primary weakness; cannot recognize/localize the left side; left leg misplaced or stuck on stairsRight (non-dominant) parietal → left hemispatial-awareness deficit
  • OSCE — describe the scan systematically. Saying only "there is a mass on the right/left" is not enough: which side? → which lobe/region? → which nearby functional structures explain the findings?

Spinal localization — past papers

These questions were filed under "Localization of lesions within the CNS" in older years. This year's slides cover brain tumours only, so the background boxes below are added to make the red facts understandable.

Added explanationRoot levels to know: C5 = shoulder abduction, biceps reflex, lateral arm (regimental badge) · C6 = lateral forearm + thumb, brachioradialis · C7 = middle finger, triceps · C8/T1 = little finger/medial forearm · T4 = nipple, T10 = umbilicus · L4 = knee jerk, medial leg · L5 = big-toe extension (EHL), lateral leg, dorsum of foot · S1 = plantar flexion, ankle jerk, lateral foot, posterior thigh/calf. A disc usually compresses the lower root at that level (L4–L5 disc → L5 root; L5–S1 disc → S1 root).
  • Middle finger sensation → C7. 438 ×2
  • Weak shoulder abduction, numbness over the lateral arm, weak biceps reflex → C5. 434 ×2
  • Hyperextension injury with C5 and C6 root injury → sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the arm and forearm. 437
  • Numbness up to the nipple (pinprick) → T4 sensory level. 437
  • Pain to the buttock, back of thigh and lateral foot, sensory loss lateral leg/foot and posterior thigh, loss of plantar flexion → L5–S1 (S1 root). 437 ×8
  • Cannot extend the big toe → L4–L5 (L5 root). 435
  • Landmark to avoid the cord during lumbar puncture → iliac crest (line joining the crests = L4; the cord ends at L1–L2). 438 ×5
Added explanationMyelopathy vs radiculopathy: cord compression (myelopathy) gives UMN signs below the level — clumsy hands, loss of fine movement, unsteady/spastic gait, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, sensory level, sphincters late. Root compression (radiculopathy) gives LMN signs in one root — dermatomal pain/numbness, weakness, lost reflex. Cauda equina = LMN, saddle anaesthesia, retention, ↓anal tone.
  • 55-year-old, unsteady gait, bilateral hand numbness, difficult fine hand movements, tandem-gait difficulty, hypertonia, brisk reflexes, positive Hoffmann → cervical myelopathy. 439 ×4
  • "Loss of fine movement" (incomplete recall) → keyed "spinal level" — the lesion is in the cord (myelopathy). 439
  • Urinary retention, two months of posterior-thigh pain, bilateral foot drop, lateral-foot sensory loss, decreased anal tone → cauda equina syndrome. 437 ×5
  • Elderly, bilateral leg numbness after walking ~15 min, leans forward on a shopping cart, normal exam → lumbar canal stenosis (neurogenic claudication). 436
  • Known prostate cancer, back pain, difficulty walking, thoracic tenderness, impaired proprioception → MRI whole spine (metastatic cord compression; image the whole spine — skip lesions). 439 ×4
  • Known IV drug user, 2 weeks of neck pain + bilateral hand numbness, normal exam → cervical spine MRI (rule out epidural abscess/discitis). 436
  • Leg numbness to the umbilicus, walking difficulty, intradural extramedullary tumour → meningioma (with schwannoma, the commonest intradural extramedullary tumours). 437 ×5
  • Child with neck pain 2 weeks after trauma (X-ray) → atlanto-axial subluxation. 437
Added explanationNeurogenic shock (cord injury above ~T6): loss of sympathetic tone → hypotension with bradycardia (or an inappropriately normal HR) and warm, dry peripheries. Treat with IV fluids, then vasopressors; always exclude haemorrhage first. Steroids (methylprednisolone) are no longer routinely recommended.
  • Fall from height, thoracic tenderness, paraplegia, BP 85/45, pulse 50 → neurogenic shock. 441 ×12
  • Unbelted MVA driver, cervical cord injury, BP 80/50 with HR 70 → first-line IV fluids and vasopressors. 442 ×2
